newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ireland hoping for deal on postal services in November.
newsitem.headline: Ireland hoping for deal on postal services in November.

text.p: The Irish presidency said on Friday that it was optimistic the Telecommunications Council would be able to break a deadlock over a plan to liberalise postal services when it meets on November 28.

Speaking after a meeting of the Council, Irish Communications Minister Michael Lowry said the ministers, who discussed the legislation over lunch, seemed committed to finding a compromise before the European Commission acts unilaterally.

The Commission has said that if the Council does not approve the draft directive on postal services, COM(95)227, by the end of 1996, it would publish a notice outlining how it would act to enforce EU competition rules in the sector.
"There was a consensus today that we should adopt a directive," Lowry told reporters.
EU member states are divided over how quickly to allow private operators to compete with state post offices to deliver direct mail and incoming cross-border mail.

The Irish presidency has proposed that direct mail be liberalised by January 1, 2001 and that ministers pledge to adopt measures by that date on further liberalisation of the sector, with particular attention to incoming cross-border mail.
But France, Belgium, Greece, Portugal and Luxembourg have resisted setting a date for liberalising direct mail, diplomats said.
Lowry said COREPER, the EU committee of permanent representatives, would continue looking for a compromise and that he would meet bilaterally with his EU counterparts if necessary.
The European Express Organisation, which represents express delivery companies, issued a statement after the meeting urging the Commission to adopt its notice on the postal sector immediately.

"The failure of the Council to make progress on the directive is a blow to consumers, particularly businesses wshich would benefit from an environment in which competitive postal services would be available," it said in a statement.

The Commission has already published a draft of the notice, which said that post offices could keep their monopolies over direct mail and incoming cross-border mail until December 31, 2000. But the Commission would decide by June 30, 1998 whether to open up competition after that date.
